title: Training intuition with master games
summary: Guess-the-move sessions: commit to a move, compare with the master, verify with calculation — and build patterns faster.

steps.md:
## Intuition is trained pattern recognition

Strong players' first impressions are usually right because they recognise thousands of patterns (chunks, templates). You build them by **active** study of master games:
1. Cover the moves; for each move of one side, **commit** to your choice (write it down or play it) before revealing.
2. Compare. If different, ask *why* the master's move is better (or whether yours was also good: check with the engine within ~0.3).
3. Calculate briefly when the position is sharp: intuition proposes, calculation verifies.
4. Score yourself; review the positions you missed a week later.

Passive replaying of games does very little. Commitment before feedback is what trains the intuition.

**Karpov-Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974**, after 23...Qd8. A model of a closed Ruy Lopez: White has space on both wings. Karpov played **24.Ba7!**, a calm move that takes the a-file away from Black's rook and freezes the queenside. Black's pieces have no squares; White then prepared f4-f5 and won on the kingside.

steps.question: In the diagram (Karpov-Unzicker 1974), what is the idea of 24.Ba7?
choices: To occupy the only open file's entry square and block the black rook on a8, so that White can later double rooks or switch to the kingside without counterplay
steps.explain: The bishop on a7 is "out of play" by normal standards but blocks the a-file completely. Intuition here is about restricting the opponent, not about piece activity rules.

steps.prompt: Guess the move. White to play (Botvinnik-Capablanca, AVRO 1938)
steps.explain: **26.Re6!** — the rook takes the open file's key square, supported by the f5-pawn; after 26...Rxe6 27.fxe6 the passed e-pawn and the queen's entry ideas give White a winning attack. Engine main line: 26.Re6 Rxe6 27.fxe6 Kg7 28.Qf4 Qa2 29.Qc7+ Kh6. (Botvinnik-Capablanca, AVRO 1938; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: Guess the move. White to play (a queenless middlegame) (Kasparov-Karpov, World Championship 1985)
steps.explain: **25.Ra4!** — the rook attacks a7 and prepares to switch along the 4th rank; Black's queenside pawns become targets. Pressure before liquidation. Engine main line: 25.Ra4 b5 26.cxb5 Rb8 27.Ke3 Rdb6 28.Ra5 Bb7. (Kasparov-Karpov, World Championship 1985; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: Guess the move. White to play (a rook and bishop ending) (Fischer-Taimanov, Candidates 1971)
steps.explain: **34.Re1!** — the rook attacks the dangerous e2-pawn from behind; only this move keeps the balance and later the winning chances. Engine main line: 34.Re1 Nd6 35.Bh5 Nb5+ 36.Kb2 g6 37.Bf3 Nd4. (Fischer-Taimanov, Candidates 1971; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.question: Your guess differs from the master's move, and the engine shows your move is only 0.1 worse. How should you score it?
choices: Zero: only the game move counts
As (nearly) correct: different but equally good moves are fine — focus your review on moves that were clearly worse
steps.explain: Engine tolerance (about 0.3 in normal positions) avoids punishing good alternatives. Spend your review time on the big differences.

steps.md:
## Assignment

- **Guess the move**: one full game per day for 2 weeks (alternate eras: one Capablanca, Karpov or Carlsen game, one Tal, Kasparov or Fischer game). Record your score.
- Every Sunday, replay the 10 positions where your guess was furthest from the master's move.
- Target at this level: within 0.3 of the master/engine move on at least 60% of moves.
